meta.headline: Chiltern Railways renationalised after 30 years as private company

relevance.reason: A privatised rail operator has returned to public ownership, which is a clear real-world case of nationalisation with figures a student can use to weigh costs and benefits.

mapping.justification: The story is about the government taking a privatised firm into public ownership, which is intervention through nationalisation.
mapping.cross_theme_note: The article also links to Theme 1 (government intervention in markets) and to Theme 4 (public expenditure and the cost to taxpayers).

paragraphs: Chiltern Railways, which runs trains from London Marylebone to Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and the West Midlands, has returned to the public sector, ending three decades as a privately run company. It was privatised in 1996. It is the tenth rail company to be brought under Great British Railways (GBR), the government's plan to take passenger rail into public hands, which the government says will save money and improve services.

The government says the change will tackle overcrowding. It plans 25 additional daily services from December, which the Department for Transport says will provide 10,000 extra seats. These include half-hourly weekday trains between London and Birmingham and more services at weekends. The operator also says new trains will improve accessibility and Wi-Fi, and passengers whose train is cancelled can now use another operator's service within two hours either side of their booked train at no extra cost.

The first day brought some disruption. A late closure of part of the West Coast Main Line, affecting services at London Euston, was expected to make the Birmingham to Marylebone route much busier, so Chiltern said it would run more trains than usual.

The rail minister said the extra trains and seats will make a real difference on a line with limited capacity, and that public ownership gives the government a chance to deliver more frequent, comfortable and punctual trains. The minister accepted that this will not happen overnight. Great Western Railway will be the next operator to move into public ownership, on 13 December, and the aim is for GBR to run all passenger services by the end of 2027.

Nationalisation changes who owns a firm and who bears its risks and costs. This article gives a real case for weighing the reasons for public ownership, such as service quality and overcrowding, against the cost to taxpayers and the risk that the government does not run the railway any better. It also shows how a government's promises can be tested against evidence.

concepts: Business objectives: profit versus service to the public
Costs and benefits of state ownership, including government failure
Capacity and overcrowding as a service quality problem
chain: The government takes Chiltern Railways, a privatised operator, into public ownership as part of Great British Railways.
The government, not private shareholders, now sets the aims of the business, so it can put reducing overcrowding and improving services ahead of making a profit.
It plans 25 extra daily services and 10,000 extra seats, which increases the capacity of the line and could make journeys less crowded.
Running extra services costs money, so the government must weigh the benefit to passengers against the cost to taxpayers, who could have paid for something else. This is the opportunity cost.
The government says public ownership will save money, but the article gives no figures, so this is a claim to test against evidence.
If services improve and costs are controlled, the case for public ownership is stronger. If costs rise or performance does not improve, it could be an example of government failure.

evaluation.label: Will the seats be used?
evaluation.text: More seats only help if passengers use them. If the extra trains run part-empty, the cost per passenger rises, so the benefit depends on demand on the line.

evaluation.label: First-day disruption
evaluation.text: The article links the disruption on the first day to the late closure of part of the West Coast Main Line, not to the change of ownership. It is a short-run problem, so it says little about how well public ownership will work in the long run.

evaluation.label: Time lags
evaluation.text: The minister accepted that the change will not happen overnight. The extra services start in December and the full transfer is not planned until the end of 2027, so the effects will take time to show.

evaluation.label: Alternatives
evaluation.text: The article does not show that public ownership is the only way to add capacity. A government could also ask a private operator to run more services, so the case rests on whether public ownership does it better or more cheaply.

evaluation.label: Who is affected
evaluation.text: Passengers may gain from more seats and help when trains are cancelled, while taxpayers would meet any extra cost. The article gives no figures on cost, so the full effect on each group is unclear.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of a private sector firm into public ownership and control.
The sale of a public sector firm or service to private owners.
Action by the state to influence how markets work, for example through regulation, taxes, subsidies or public ownership.
The part of the economy that is owned and run by the government.
The main aim of a firm, such as maximising profit or providing a service.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
When intervention by the government leads to a less efficient use of resources than would have happened without it.
The maximum number of passengers or amount of output that a service can carry or produce.

questions.prompt: The government plans 25 additional daily services from December, and the Department for Transport says the additional services will provide 10,000 extra seats. Assuming the extra seats come from the 25 additional services, how many extra seats does each additional service provide on average?
Private train operators usually aim to make a profit. Which change described in the article best shows the government using public ownership to pursue a different objective?

options.text: Charging higher fares to raise revenue
Adding 25 daily services to ease crowding
Running fewer trains to cut costs

questions.explanation: The extra services are meant to tackle overcrowding, which is a service objective. The other options are ways of raising profit or cutting costs, or the opposite of nationalisation.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the move of Chiltern Railways from a private company into government ownership?
questions.explanation: Nationalisation is the transfer of a private sector firm into public ownership. Privatisation is the reverse.

questions.prompt: Explain one possible benefit of bringing Chiltern Railways into public ownership.

points: Identifies a valid benefit of public ownership, such as putting passengers' interests ahead of profit or being able to plan services across the network.
Uses the article, for example the 25 additional daily services from December, the 10,000 extra seats or the half-hourly weekday trains between London and Birmingham.
Refers to the government's stated aims of tackling overcrowding and improving services.
Develops a chain, for example: the government can set aims other than profit (1), so it can add services and seats that reduce overcrowding and improve journeys for passengers (1).

notes: Award a mark for each stage of a chain that is explained, up to the marks available.

questions.prompt: Assess whether bringing rail operators such as Chiltern Railways into public ownership is likely to benefit passengers and taxpayers.

points: Nationalisation is the transfer of a private firm into public ownership.
Public ownership allows the government to pursue aims other than profit, such as service quality.
Public money spent on rail has an opportunity cost.
Chiltern was privatised in 1996 and is the tenth company to join Great British Railways.
25 additional daily services and 10,000 extra seats from December.
The government says public ownership will save money, but the article gives no figures.
Disruption on the first day, caused by the West Coast Main Line closure.
The aim for Great British Railways to run all passenger services by the end of 2027, with Great Western Railway next on 13 December.

For: public ownership lets the government add services and seats, so overcrowding falls, and it can improve service quality, for example by letting passengers with cancelled trains use another operator's service at no extra cost.

Against: extra services and seats cost money that taxpayers pay and that could have been spent elsewhere. With no figures on savings, costs could rise without better service, which would be government failure because resources are used less efficiently than before.
Judge using the evidence: the article gives aims and extra capacity but no figures on cost or savings.
Consider the time lag: extra services start in December and the full transfer is planned for the end of 2027, so the benefits may take time to appear.
Consider who gains and who pays: passengers gain capacity, taxpayers may bear the cost, and first-day disruption shows change is not risk free.

A supported conclusion states a clear view, for example that public ownership is likely to help passengers if the extra services are delivered, but that taxpayers gain only if costs are controlled and savings are shown.

discussion.prompt: Should railways be run by the government or by private companies, and what evidence would help you decide?

points.label: The government's case
points.text: Public ownership is meant to save money, improve services and tackle overcrowding.

points.label: What is planned for passengers
points.text: More frequent weekday trains between London and Birmingham, new trains that the operator says will improve accessibility and Wi-Fi, and the right to use another operator's service if a train is cancelled.

points.label: What comes next
points.text: Great Western Railway is the next operator to move, on 13 December. The aim is for all passenger services to be run by Great British Railways by the end of 2027.
